questions.question: Which among the following measures was introduced by Muhammad bin Tughlaq to address the shortage of silver?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Token currency**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In **1329-1330 AD**, **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** introduced a **Token Currency** system to manage the severe global shortage of **silver** bullion during the 14th century.
 
• The Sultan issued coins made of base metals, specifically **brass** and **copper**, and decreed that they should be accepted at the same value as the silver **Tanka**.
 
• The primary objective was to preserve the state's **silver reserves** while maintaining a high level of liquidity for his ambitious military projects and administrative expenses.
 
• The idea was modeled after the successful use of paper currency (**Chao**) in **China** under **Kublai Khan** and similar experiments in **Persia** (Gaykhatu Khan).
 
• However, the experiment failed because the government could not prevent **forgery**; households reportedly began minting their own copper coins, leading to massive **inflation** and a total collapse of the credit system.
 
• To restore order, the Sultan had to withdraw the token coins and exchange them for genuine **silver** and **gold** coins from the royal treasury, resulting in a massive financial loss.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**:

 
 
• He is often referred to by historians as the **Prince of Moneyers** because of the high quality and variety of coins he produced during his reign.
 
• His other controversial projects included the **transfer of the capital** from **Delhi** to **Devagiri** (renamed **Daulatabad**) in **1327 AD**.
 
 
 
• **Land Revenue Reforms**:
 
 
• While he did introduce heavy taxation in the **Doab** region to increase state revenue, this was aimed at funding his large standing army rather than directly addressing the **bullion shortage**.
 
 
 
• **Garrison Towns**:
 
 
• These were fortified settlements with soldiers, a concept more associated with the military control strategies of earlier Sultans like **Ghiyasuddin Balban** and **Alauddin Khalji** to defend against **Mongol** invasions.

questions.question: The Constitution (88th) Amendment Act, 2003, is related to which tax?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Service Tax**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Constitution (88th Amendment) Act, 2003**, was enacted to provide a formal constitutional framework for the levy and collection of **Service Tax** in India.
 
• Prior to this amendment, service tax was collected by the **Union Government** using its residuary powers under **Entry 97** of the **Union List** (List I) since **1994**.
 
• The amendment resulted in the insertion of **Article 268A**, which explicitly empowered the **Government of India** to levy taxes on services, while the appropriation of the revenue was to be shared between the **Union** and the **States**.
 
• It also expanded the **Seventh Schedule** of the Constitution by adding **Entry 92C** (Taxes on Services) to the **Union List**.
 
• This legislative step was crucial for formalizing the sharing of service tax proceeds between different levels of government, following the recommendations of various tax reform committees like the **Chelliah Committee**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Goods and Services Tax (GST)**:

 
 
• Introduced through the **101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016**, it completely overhauled the indirect tax regime in India.
 
• The **GST** subsumed **Service Tax**, **Excise Duty**, and **VAT**, leading to the repeal of **Article 268A** and **Entry 92C** that were introduced by the 88th Amendment.
 
 
 
• **Wealth Tax**:
 
 
• Governed by the **Wealth-tax Act, 1957**, it was a **Direct Tax** on the net wealth of certain entities.
 
• The government abolished wealth tax in the **Union Budget 2015**, replacing it with an additional **2% surcharge** on individuals with a taxable income exceeding 1 crore rupees.
 
 
 
• **Property Tax**:
 
 
• A local tax levied by **Municipal Corporations** or **Local Bodies** on real estate, based on the annual rental value or capital value of the property.

questions.question: Seleucus sent his ambassador Megasthenes to the court of which Mauryan ruler at Pataliputra?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chandragupta Maurya**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Megasthenes** was an ancient **Greek** historian, diplomat, and explorer who served as the official ambassador of **Seleucus I Nicator**, the founder of the **Seleucid Empire**.
 
• Following the **Seleucid–Mauryan war** (approximately **305–303 BCE**), a peace treaty was concluded between **Seleucus I** and **Chandragupta Maurya**, which involved territorial exchanges and a matrimonial alliance.
 
• As a consequence of this diplomatic reconciliation, **Megasthenes** was sent to the Mauryan capital, **Pataliputra**, to represent the Greeks in the royal court of **Chandragupta Maurya**.
 
• During his tenure at the court, he authored the seminal work titled **Indica**, which serves as a vital primary source for understanding the **Mauryan administration**, the seven-fold caste system, and the urban layout of **Pataliputra**.
 
• His accounts provide the earliest systematic description of **Indian society** and the military strength of the **Mauryan Empire** by a foreign observer.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chandragupta Maurya**:

 
 
• He was the founder of the **Mauryan Dynasty** (reigned c. **321–297 BCE**) and is credited with unifying most of the Indian subcontinent under a single central authority with the guidance of **Chanakya**.
 
 
 
• **Bindusara**:
 
 
• The son of Chandragupta Maurya; during his reign, the Greek king **Antiochus I** sent an ambassador named **Deimachus** to the Mauryan court.
 
 
 
• **Ashoka**:
 
 
• The third Mauryan emperor, famous for his conversion to **Buddhism**; historical records suggest that **Dionysius** was the Greek ambassador sent to his court by **Ptolemy II Philadelphus**.
 
 
 
• **Brihadratha**:
 
 
• The last ruler of the **Mauryan Empire**, who was assassinated by his general **Pushyamitra Shunga** in **185 BCE**, leading to the rise of the **Shunga Dynasty**.

questions.question: What was the theme of the 10th National Consultation conducted on 11-12 October 2025?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Safeguarding the Girl Child**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **10th National Consultation** on Child Protection was organized by the **Supreme Court Juvenile Justice Committee** in collaboration with **UNICEF India** on **October 11-12, 2025**.
 
• The event was specifically themed **Safeguarding the Girl Child** to coincide with the **International Day of the Girl Child**, which is observed globally on **October 11** every year.
 
• The primary objective of the consultation was to evaluate the implementation of the **Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012**, and the **Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015**, with a specific focus on the unique vulnerabilities faced by girls.
 
• Key stakeholders, including **High Court Judges**, representatives from the **Ministry of Women and Child Development**, and child rights advocates, discussed strategies to enhance **gender-sensitive** legal procedures and rehabilitation frameworks.
 
• The consultation emphasized the urgency of addressing the backlog of **POCSO cases** in **Special Courts** and ensuring the **privacy and dignity** of girl survivors during trial proceedings.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **International Day of the Girl Child**:

 
 
• Declared by the **United Nations** in **2011**, this day aims to highlight and address the needs and challenges girls face while promoting **girl empowerment** and the fulfillment of their **human rights**.
 
• The 2025 consultation utilized this global platform to push for structural changes in India’s **Child Protection Services (CPS)**.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Oversight**:
 
 
• The **Supreme Court of India** plays a pivotal role in monitoring the **Juvenile Justice system** through these annual consultations, ensuring that **Special Juvenile Police Units (SJPUs)** and **Child Welfare Committees (CWCs)** are functioning effectively.
 
• Previous themes have focused on the **digital safety** of children and the prevention of **child trafficking**, but the 10th edition prioritized the comprehensive safety of girls in both domestic and institutional settings.

questions.question: The dominant sights at Lothal are the ________, which have helped make this place so important to international archaeology.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dockyards**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Lothal**, located in the **Bhal** region of modern-day **Gujarat**, is world-famous for possessing the **earliest known artificial dockyard**, which dates back to approximately **2400 BCE**.
 
• The dockyard is a sophisticated rectangular basin made of **kiln-burnt bricks**, measuring roughly **214 meters** in length and **36 meters** in width, connected to the ancient course of the **Sabarmati River**.
 
• This structure was engineered with a **sluice gate** system to control the flow of water and maintain the water level during **low tides**, showcasing the advanced **hydrographic knowledge** of the **Indus Valley Civilization (IVC)**.
 
• The presence of the dockyard established Lothal as a premier **maritime trade center**, linking the Harappan civilization with distant lands such as **Mesopotamia (Sumer)**, **Egypt**, and the **Persian Gulf**.
 
• Excavations led by archaeologist **S.R. Rao** in **1954** revealed that this dockyard facilitated the export of luxury items like **carnelian beads**, **ivory**, and **copper**, which were highly valued in international markets.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Other Archaeological Features at Lothal:**

 
 
• **Bead-Making Factory:** Lothal was a major industrial hub for the production of **micro-beads** and gemstone ornaments, featuring a specialized factory with a working platform.
 
• **Rice Husk:** Evidence of **rice cultivation** was found here, which is relatively rare in other major Harappan sites.
 
• **Persian Gulf Seals:** The discovery of **circular button-shaped seals** indicates direct maritime contact with the **Dilmun** civilization (modern-day Bahrain).
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Options:**
 
 
• **Great Baths:** This iconic structure is the hallmark of **Mohenjo-daro**, primarily used for ritualistic bathing rather than trade.
 
• **Citadels:** While most IVC cities, including Lothal, had a **Citadel** (upper town) for the ruling class, it is not the unique feature that defines Lothal's international importance.
 
• **Granaries:** Massive **Granaries** for surplus food storage were the dominant features of **Harappa** and **Mohenjo-daro**, serving as the state treasury.

questions.question: When was national Agriculture policy launched in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2000**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **National Agriculture Policy (NAP)** was officially announced by the **Government of India** on **July 28, 2000**. It was the first-ever comprehensive policy formulated to steer the country's agricultural sector into the new millennium.
 
• The central objective of the policy was to achieve a growth rate of over **4 percent per annum** in the agriculture sector. This growth was intended to be sustainable, technologically driven, and demand-oriented.
 
• The policy introduced the concept of the **Rainbow Revolution**, which aimed to integrate various specialized revolutions like the **Green Revolution** (food grains), **White Revolution** (milk), **Yellow Revolution** (oilseeds), **Blue Revolution** (fisheries), **Red Revolution** (meat and poultry), and **Golden Revolution** (fruits and honey).
 
• It emphasized **'Growth with Equity'**, focusing on regional balance and ensuring that the benefits of agricultural development reached small and marginal farmers across all geographical areas of **India**.
 
• The **NAP 2000** encouraged the involvement of the **private sector** through **contract farming** and land leasing arrangements to facilitate accelerated technology transfer, capital inflow, and a steady market for agricultural produce.
 
• The policy aimed at protecting **plant varieties** through a specialized sui generis system and promoting the use of **biotechnology** for developing improved seed varieties and sustainable farming practices.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **National Policy for Farmers (NPF), 2007**:

 
 
• While the **2000 policy** focused on agricultural production, the **2007 policy** (approved based on the recommendations of the **National Commission on Farmers** chaired by **Dr. M.S. Swaminathan**) shifted the focus toward the **well-being of the farmers** and improving their net income.
 
• It introduced the concept of **'Income Security'** for farmers as a primary goal.
 
 
 
• **Resource Management**:
 
 
• The **National Agriculture Policy 2000** highlighted the importance of conserving **biodiversity** and the sustainable management of **natural resources** like land and water.
 
• It prioritized **integrated pest management (IPM)** and **integrated nutrient management (INM)** to reduce the chemical footprint on the environment.

questions.question: Which historical policy skewed China’s gender ratio at birth?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**One-Child Policy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **One-Child Policy** was a rigorous population control program introduced by the **Chinese government** in **1979** to curb the country's rapid population growth.
 
• Deep-seated cultural traditions in **China** historically favored **male heirs** for agricultural labor, carrying on the family lineage, and providing **social security** for elderly parents.
 
• Under the strict limitation of a single child, many families resorted to **sex-selective abortion**, **female infanticide**, and **abandonment** of girls to ensure their only legal child was a boy.
 
• This demographic engineering led to a severely skewed **Sex Ratio at Birth (SRB)**; while the natural ratio is roughly 105 boys to 100 girls, China's ratio peaked at approximately **118 to 120 males** for every 100 females in the early **21st century**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The policy was formally ended in **2015**, transitioning first to a **two-child policy** in **2016** and subsequently to a **three-child policy** in **2021** to mitigate the crisis of an **aging population** and **labor shortages**.
 
• Impact of other options:
 
 
• **Universal Healthcare Act**: Refers to policies ensuring **medical access** for all citizens, which generally improves overall **life expectancy** rather than skewing birth ratios.
 
• **Gender Equity Law**: These legal frameworks are designed to **eliminate discrimination** and protect women's rights, which typically works toward balancing social disparities.
 
• **Rural Migration Ban**: Often associated with the **Hukou system**, this policy restricted **internal migration** from villages to cities but did not dictate reproductive outcomes or gender selection.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India grants the “Right to Constitutional Remedies,” empowering individuals to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 32**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 32** of the **Indian Constitution** provides the **Right to Constitutional Remedies**, which allows citizens to approach the **Supreme Court** for the enforcement of **Fundamental Rights** listed in **Part III**.
 
• **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**, the architect of the Constitution, described this article as the **'Heart and Soul of the Constitution'** because it makes all other rights functional and enforceable.
 
• The **Supreme Court** is designated as the **protector and guarantor** of Fundamental Rights under this provision, ensuring that the State does not infringe upon individual liberties.
 
• The Article empowers the court to issue five types of **prerogative writs**: **Habeas Corpus**, **Mandamus**, **Prohibition**, **Certiorari**, and **Quo-Warranto**.
 
• This right cannot be suspended except as provided by the Constitution, specifically during a **National Emergency** under **Article 359** by the President.
 
• Because it is vital to the constitutional structure, the **Supreme Court** has ruled that **Article 32** is a **basic feature** of the Constitution, meaning it cannot be abridged or taken away even by a constitutional amendment.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 226**:

 
 
• Empowers the **High Courts** to issue writs for the enforcement of **Fundamental Rights** and for 'any other purpose', giving it a broader jurisdiction than the Supreme Court in this specific regard.
 
 
 
• **Article 21**:
 
 
• Guarantees the **Protection of Life and Personal Liberty**, stating that no person shall be deprived of their life or liberty except according to **procedure established by law**.
 
• It has been widely interpreted by the judiciary to include rights like **privacy**, **clean environment**, and **legal aid**.
 
 
 
• **Article 19**:
 
 
• Protects six basic freedoms for citizens: **speech and expression**, peaceful assembly, formation of associations, movement throughout India, residence, and practicing any profession.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution provides free legal aid to the poor and weaker sections of the society?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 39 A**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 39 A** is a significant provision under the **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**, which are contained in **Part IV** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• This article was inserted by the **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976**, during the emergency period to promote **equal justice** and **free legal aid**.
 
• The provision directs the State to ensure that the legal system operates in a manner that promotes **justice** on the basis of **equal opportunity** for all citizens.
 
• It specifically mandates the State to provide **free legal aid** through suitable legislation or schemes to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of **economic** or other **disabilities**.
 
• To fulfill the constitutional mandate of this Article, the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** was enacted, which led to the establishment of the **National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)** to monitor and implement legal aid programs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 29**:

 
 
• Falls under **Part III** (Fundamental Rights) and deals with the **Protection of interests of minorities**.
 
• It grants any section of citizens residing in India the right to conserve their distinct **language, script, or culture**.
 
 
 
• **Article 51 A**:
 
 
• Contained in **Part IV-A**, it lists the **Fundamental Duties** of Indian citizens.
 
• Originally, ten duties were added by the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, and an eleventh was added by the **86th Amendment Act, 2002**.
 
 
 
• **Article 78**:
 
 
• Specifies the **Duties of the Prime Minister** regarding the furnishing of information to the **President**.
 
• It mandates the PM to communicate all decisions of the **Council of Ministers** related to the administration of the Union and proposals for legislation to the President.

questions.question: Ustad Bismillah Khan was most closely associated with which musical instrument?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Shehnai**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ustad Bismillah Khan** (1916–2006) was a legendary Indian musician who is credited with single-handedly elevating the **Shehnai** from a traditional folk and wedding instrument to the global classical concert stage.
 
• Born as **Qamaruddin Khan** in **Dumraon**, **Bihar**, he came from a lineage of court musicians; he received his training in **Varanasi** under his maternal uncle, **Ali Baksh 'Vilayatu'**, a prominent Shehnai player at the **Kashi Vishwanath Temple**.
 
• He is celebrated for his historic performance at the **Red Fort** on **15th August 1947**, where his music greeted the nation on the eve of **Indian Independence** at the invitation of **Jawaharlal Nehru**.
 
• He was a symbol of India's **composite culture** (Ganga-Jamuni Tehzeeb) and received the **Bharat Ratna**, India's highest civilian award, in **2001**.
 
• Throughout his career, he was honored with numerous accolades including the **Padma Shri** (1961), **Padma Bhushan** (1968), and **Padma Vibhushan** (1980).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Shehnai**:

 
 
• A **double-reed aerophone** common in India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh; it features a wooden body and a flared metal bell.
 
 
 
• **Tabla**:
 
 
• A pair of twin hand drums (the **Dayan** and **Bayan**) fundamental to **Hindustani classical music**; famous maestros include **Ustad Zakir Hussain** and **Pandit Kishan Maharaj**.
 
 
 
• **Sarod**:
 
 
• A fretless string instrument with a deep, resonant tone; it is a vital part of the Indian classical tradition, mastered by **Ustad Amjad Ali Khan** and **Ustad Ali Akbar Khan**.
 
 
 
• **Sitar**:
 
 
• A plucked string instrument known for its complex sympathetic strings; it gained worldwide fame through **Pandit Ravi Shankar** and **Ustad Vilayat Khan**.

questions.question: Which region in India is best known for slash-and-burn agriculture (jhum)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**North-Eastern Hills**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Slash-and-burn agriculture**, locally known as **Jhum** or **Jhumming**, is a primitive form of **shifting cultivation** widely practiced in the **North-Eastern Hills** of India, encompassing states like **Assam**, **Meghalaya**, **Mizoram**, and **Nagaland**.
 
• The process involves clearing a patch of **forest land** by cutting down vegetation and burning it; the resulting **ash** provides essential nutrients to the soil for crop production.
 
• Farmers typically cultivate crops like **dry paddy**, **buckwheat**, **maize**, and **millets** for a few years until **soil fertility** declines, after which the land is left **fallow** to recover naturally.
 
• This agricultural system is deeply integrated into the **tribal culture** and socio-economic life of the **North-Eastern region**, though it is increasingly being regulated due to **environmental concerns** like deforestation and soil erosion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Regional nomenclature of shifting cultivation:**

 
 
• **Western Ghats**: In the hilly regions of the **Western Ghats** (specifically **Kerala** and **Karnataka**), this practice is known as **Kumari**.
 
• **Central India**: It is called **Bewar** or **Dahiya** in **Madhya Pradesh**, and **Podu** or **Penda** in **Andhra Pradesh** and **Odisha**.
 
• **Himalayan Belt**: The practice is referred to as **Khil** in the **Himalayan** range.
 
• **South-East Rajasthan**: It is known as **Valre** or **Waltre** in this arid/semi-arid region.
 
 
 
• **Global nomenclature:**
 
 
• In **Mexico** and **Central America**, it is called **Milpa**.
 
• In **Vietnam**, it is known as **Ray**, and in **Indonesia/Malaysia**, it is termed **Ladang**.
 
 
 
• The **Indo-Gangetic Plain** and the **Deccan Plateau** are primarily known for **intensive subsistence farming** and **commercial agriculture** respectively, rather than slash-and-burn methods, due to their distinct **topography** and high **population density**.

questions.question: Which of the following states has high population density due to early human settlement and development?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Uttar Pradesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Uttar Pradesh** is situated in the fertile **Indo-Gangetic Plain**, a region characterized by rich **alluvial soil** and an abundance of perennial water sources like the **Ganges** and **Yamuna** rivers.
 
• Historically, this region served as the cradle of early **human settlements** in South Asia, including the center of the **Vedic civilization** and several **Mahajanapadas** (powerful ancient kingdoms), which fostered high population concentrations over millennia.
 
• The **flat topography** of the state facilitated the easy development of transport networks, agriculture, and permanent housing, leading to a long-standing pattern of high-density habitation.
 
• According to the **2011 Census**, Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state in India, with a **population density** of **829 persons per square kilometer**, which is significantly higher than the national average.
 
• The continuous availability of **arable land** and a favorable climate for **double-cropping** have historically supported large agrarian societies, ensuring food security and sustained population growth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rajasthan**:

 
 
• Much of its territory is covered by the **Thar Desert**, where extreme temperatures and **water scarcity** historically limited the density of human settlements.
 
• Despite being the largest state by area, its population density is much lower than that of the northern plains.
 
 
 
• **Sikkim and Meghalaya**:
 
 
• These states are located in the **Himalayan** and **North-Eastern hilly regions**, respectively.
 
• **Rugged terrain**, steep slopes, and **dense forest cover** pose significant challenges for large-scale agriculture and infrastructure development, resulting in **sparse population** distribution.
 
• Sikkim is notably the least populous state in India, reflecting the constraints of high-altitude geography on human settlement.

questions.question: Which part of the small intestine in the human digestive system receives bile from the gall bladder and pancreatic juice from the pancreas through a common bile duct?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Duodenum**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Duodenum** is the first and shortest segment of the **small intestine**, measuring approximately **20 to 25 cm** in length and exhibiting a characteristic **C-shape**.
 
• It is the critical site where the **stomach** empties its acidic **chyme** to be mixed with alkaline digestive secretions from the accessory organs.
 
• The **common bile duct** (transporting bile from the **liver** and **gall bladder**) and the **main pancreatic duct** (carrying **pancreatic juice**) converge to form the **hepatopancreatic ampulla**, also known as the **Ampulla of Vater**.
 
• This ampulla opens into the second part of the **duodenum** through a structure called the **major duodenal papilla**, which is regulated by the **Sphincter of Oddi**.
 
• The **bile** received here is essential for the **emulsification of fats**, while the **pancreatic juice** provides enzymes like **trypsin**, **lipase**, and **amylase** along with **bicarbonate ions** to neutralize gastric acid.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Jejunum**

questions.question: In a laboratory, copper sulphate solution reacts with iron filings, causing a colour change and the deposition of a new metal. Which statement correctly explains the reason for this reaction?

options.text: Copper is more reactive than iron
Iron and copper sulphate have similar reactivity
Iron and copper belong to the same group
Iron is more reactive than copper

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Iron is more reactive than copper**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The reaction between **iron filings** and **copper sulphate solution** is a classic example of a **single displacement reaction**, where a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound.
 
• According to the **reactivity series** of metals, **Iron (Fe)** is positioned above **Copper (Cu)**, indicating that iron is more chemically active and has a higher tendency to lose electrons.
 
• When iron is added to the **blue-coloured** copper sulphate solution (**CuSO₄**), it displaces the copper ions to form **ferrous sulphate (FeSO₄)** and solid copper metal.
 
• The chemical equation for this reaction is represented as: **Fe (s) + CuSO₄ (aq) → FeSO₄ (aq) + Cu (s)**.
 
• The observation of the solution changing from **blue** to **light green** confirms the formation of **Fe²⁺ ions** in the form of ferrous sulphate.
 
• The **reddish-brown deposit** seen on the iron filings is the pure **copper metal** that has been displaced from the solution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Reactivity Series**:

 
 
• It is an arrangement of metals in the decreasing order of their **reactivity**. Metals at the top, like **Potassium (K)** and **Sodium (Na)**, are highly reactive, while those at the bottom, like **Gold (Au)** and **Platinum (Pt)**, are least reactive.
 
• **Iron** is more reactive than **Tin (Sn)**, **Lead (Pb)**, and **Copper (Cu)**, allowing it to displace these metals from their respective salt solutions.
 
 
 
• **Displacement Constraints**:
 
 
• A reaction will not occur if a less reactive metal is added to a solution of a more reactive metal's salt; for instance, **copper** cannot displace **iron** from **iron sulphate**.
 
• **Iron** belongs to **Group 8** and **Period 4** of the **Periodic Table**, whereas **Copper** belongs to **Group 11** and **Period 4**. Although they are both **transition metals**, their electronic configurations result in different levels of chemical reactivity.

questions.question: Which Constitutional Article was primarily referenced by the Supreme Court in the declaration of maternity leave being a constitutional right even for a third child, in May 2025?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 21**__.

__
 
• In **May 2025**, the **Supreme Court of India** passed a significant judgment clarifying that the right to **maternity leave** is an intrinsic part of **Article 21** of the **Indian Constitution**, which guarantees the **Protection of Life and Personal Liberty**.
 
• The Court held that the right to **reproduce** and the right to **maternal health** are fundamental components of a woman's **dignity** and **bodily autonomy**, which cannot be curtailed by the state or employers based on the number of children.
 
• The ruling addressed various state service rules that previously restricted **maternity benefits** to only the first two children. The Court declared such restrictions **unconstitutional**, stating that the **biological reality** of childbirth and the necessity of **infant care** do not change with the **third child**.
 
• The bench emphasized that **Article 21** must be read in conjunction with the **Maternity Benefit Act, 1961**, to ensure that **social security** measures fulfill the constitutional goal of **gender justice** and **economic empowerment** for women in the workforce.
 
• By linking maternity leave to the **Right to Life**, the judiciary ensured that women are not forced to choose between their **fundamental right to employment** and their **reproductive rights**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 14**:

 
 
• Guarantees **Equality before the law** and **equal protection of laws** within the territory of India.
 
• While it prohibits **arbitrary classification**, the primary focus of the 2025 declaration was the **inherent dignity** and **survival rights** found under the umbrella of **Article 21**.
 
 
 
• **Article 19**:
 
 
• Protects the six **Fundamental Freedoms**, including speech, assembly, and **profession**.
 
• Although maternity leave impacts the right to practice a profession, it is categorized under **protective discrimination** and **right to health** rather than mere freedom of movement or expression.
 
 
 
• **Article 27**:
 
 
• Provides **Freedom as to payment of taxes** for the promotion of any particular religion.
 
• This article is entirely unrelated to **labor welfare**, **reproductive rights**, or **constitutional mandates** for maternity benefits.
 
 
 
• **Article 42**:
 
 
• A **Directive Principle of State Policy (DPSP)** that mandates the state to make provisions for **just and humane conditions of work** and **maternity relief**.
 
• It serves as the **interpretative guide** that the Supreme Court used to expand the functional scope of **Article 21** in this context.

questions.question: Which mountain range in India is one of the oldest fold mountains in the world?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Aravalli Range**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Aravalli Range** is an ancient mountain system in **Northwestern India**, stretching approximately **670 kilometers** across the states of **Gujarat**, **Rajasthan**, **Haryana**, and the Union Territory of **Delhi**.
 
• It is globally recognized as one of the **oldest fold mountain** systems, with its geological origins dating back to the **Proterozoic Eon**, approximately **2.5 billion years** ago.
 
• The range was formed during the **Aravalli-Delhi Orogeny** in the **Precambrian** era, making it significantly older than the **Himalayas**, which are classified as young fold mountains.
 
• Due to continuous **weathering** and **erosion** over millions of years, the Aravallis are now categorized as **relict mountains** (residual mountains), characterized by rounded peaks and lower elevations.
 
• The highest point of this range is **Guru Shikhar**, located on **Mount Abu** in Rajasthan, which stands at an elevation of **1,722 meters** above sea level.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Himalayas**:

 
 
• Known as **Young Fold Mountains**, they formed about **50 million years** ago due to the collision of the **Indian** and **Eurasian** plates.
 
• They contain the world's highest peaks, including **Mount Everest** and **Kanchenjunga**.
 
 
 
• **Karakoram Range**:
 
 
• Part of the **Trans-Himalayan** mountain system, it is home to **K2** (Godwin-Austen), the second-highest peak in the world.
 
• It is a geologically active and young range situated in the **Gilgit-Baltistan** and **Ladakh** regions.
 
 
 
• **Eastern Ghats**:
 
 
• A discontinuous chain of mountains along India's **eastern coast**, spanning through **Odisha**, **Andhra Pradesh**, and **Tamil Nadu**.
 
• They are older than the **Western Ghats** but younger than the **Aravallis**, primarily composed of **metamorphic rocks** like **khondalites** and **charnockites**.

questions.question: When you choose 'Shut down' in Windows, what happens?

options.text: The PC enters a low-power state but keeps apps in memory
All apps and data are closed and the PC powers off completely
The PC goes into stand-by mode
The PC saves the session to the disk and then powers off

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**All apps and data are closed and the PC powers off completely**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Shut down** command in **Windows** initiates a sequence that gracefully terminates all active software **processes** and **services**.
 
• When this option is selected, the **Operating System** sends a signal to all open **applications** to close; if there is unsaved data, **Windows** typically prompts the user to save their work before proceeding.
 
• Unlike other power modes, a full **Shut down** flushes the **Random Access Memory (RAM)** entirely, ensuring that no temporary session data remains in the volatile memory.
 
• Once all software components are closed and the **Windows Kernel** is stopped, the motherboard sends a signal to the **Power Supply Unit (PSU)** to cease the flow of electricity to the **CPU**, **Hard Drives**, and other peripherals.
 
• This process is essential for hardware maintenance, installing certain updates, and clearing system **cache** or memory leaks that may have occurred during the session.
 
• Therefore, the correct option is 2.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sleep Mode (Stand-by)**:

 
 
• This is a **low-power state** that keeps the current session, including all open **apps** and **files**, stored in the **RAM**.
 
• It allows the computer to resume full-power operation within seconds, but it requires a small amount of electricity to maintain the data in **volatile memory**.
 
 
 
• **Hibernation**:
 
 
• Primarily designed for **laptops**, this mode saves the current state of the system to the **Hard Disk** or **SSD** in a file named **hiberfil.sys**.
 
• After saving the session to the disk, the PC powers off completely, consuming zero power while allowing the user to resume exactly where they left off.
 
 
 
• **Restart**:
 
 
• This function closes all **applications**, shuts down the **Operating System**, and then immediately reboots the machine. It is frequently used to finalize **software installations** or **driver updates**.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is NOT correct regarding the Indian Desert (Thar Desert)?

• The **Great Indian Desert**, commonly known as the **Thar Desert**, is situated towards the western margins of the **Aravali Hills**. The range acts as a climatic divide, keeping the western part dry. *Hence, statement 1 is correct.*
 
• This region is characterized by an **arid climate** with extremely low precipitation. While the rainfall is indeed low, it typically averages between **100 mm and 150 mm** per year (not below 15 mm). *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*
 
• It is geologically believed that the **Thar Desert** was under the sea during the **Mesozoic era**. This is supported by **marine deposits** and **wood fossils** discovered in regions like **Akal** near Jaisalmer, which date back to about 180 million years. *Hence, statement 3 is correct.*
 
• The desert features an **undulating sandy plain** covered with sand dunes. Due to high evaporation and low moisture, it has **low vegetation cover** consisting mostly of xerophytic plants. *Hence, statement 4 is correct.*

questions.question: The process of growth and healing in the body is supported by which food component?

__
 
• **Proteins** are large, complex molecules known as the **building blocks** of the human body, composed of smaller units called **amino acids**. There are **20 different amino acids** that combine in various sequences to form proteins.
 
• In the process of **growth**, proteins are essential for the production of **new cells** and the expansion of muscle mass, skin, and organs, especially during **childhood**, **adolescence**, and **pregnancy**.
 
• For **healing** and **tissue repair**, the body utilizes proteins to synthesize **collagen**, which provides the structural framework for skin and bones, and **fibrin**, which is necessary for **blood clotting** and wound closure.
 
• Beyond structure, proteins serve as **enzymes** and **hormones** (like **insulin**) that catalyze metabolic reactions and regulate physiological processes necessary for maintaining homeostasis.
 
• While the body can use proteins for energy, providing approximately **4 kcal per gram**, their primary biological priority is the **maintenance** and **regeneration** of damaged tissues.

• These are **organic micronutrients** required in trace amounts to facilitate chemical reactions, such as **Vitamin C** for **immune function** and **Vitamin K** for bone metabolism.

questions.question: The speed at which a Central Processing Unit (CPU) executes instructions is primarily determined by its clock rate, which is typically measured in gigahertz (GHz). If a CPU has a clock rate of 3.5 GHz, approximately how many clock cycles occur every second?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**3.5 billion cycles per sec**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Clock Rate** (or clock speed) refers to the frequency at which a **Central Processing Unit (CPU)** executes its most basic operations, such as adding two numbers or moving data between registers.
 
• Clock speed is measured using the **Hertz (Hz)** unit, where **1 Hz** is defined as one cycle per second.
 
• The prefix **Giga (G)** in the metric system represents a factor of **10⁹**, which is equivalent to **1,000,000,000** (one billion).
 
• Consequently, **1 Gigahertz (GHz)** means the processor performs one billion clock cycles every second.
 
• For a CPU with a clock rate of **3.5 GHz**, the calculation is 3.5 × 10⁹, which equals **3,500,000,000 cycles per second**.
 
• This measurement indicates the internal speed at which the **System Clock** oscillates to synchronize the components of the computer.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Understanding Metric Prefixes in Computing:
 
 
• **Kilohertz (kHz)**: Represents 1,000 (one thousand) cycles per second. Early computing devices often operated in this range.
 
• **Megahertz (MHz)**: Represents 1,000,000 (one million) cycles per second. This was the standard unit for processors during the **1980s and 1990s** (e.g., the **Intel 80486**).
 
• **Gigahertz (GHz)**: The current standard for modern **CPUs**, **RAM (Random Access Memory)**, and **GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)** speeds.
 
 
 
• The **Fetch-Decode-Execute** cycle:
 
 
• The speed of this cycle is directly limited by the clock rate; higher GHz generally allows more instructions to be processed in the same timeframe.
 
• Modern CPUs often employ **Overclocking**, which involves increasing the clock rate beyond the factory settings to enhance performance, though this generates significant heat.
 
• Efficiency is also measured by **IPC (Instructions Per Cycle)**, meaning a CPU with a lower clock rate but higher IPC might outperform a high-GHz processor.

questions.question: The discovery of the atomic nucleus by bombarding a thin gold foil with alpha particles is associated with which of the following scientists?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ernest Rutherford**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In **1911**, the British physicist **Ernest Rutherford** conducted the landmark **Gold Foil Experiment** (also known as the **Geiger-Marsden experiment**) to probe the structure of the atom.
 
• He bombarded a very thin sheet of **gold foil**, approximately **1000 atoms thick**, with high-energy, positively charged **alpha particles** (doubly ionized helium nuclei).
 
• While most particles passed straight through the foil, Rutherford observed that a small fraction was deflected by large angles, and approximately **1 in 12,000 particles** rebounded almost **180 degrees**.
 
• Rutherford concluded that the atom is mostly **empty space** and contains a tiny, dense, and **positively charged center** called the **nucleus**, which contains nearly all of the atom's **mass**.
 
• This discovery effectively disproved the **Plum Pudding Model** proposed by **J.J. Thomson**, leading to the development of the **Rutherford Atomic Model**.
 
• Therefore, **Ernest Rutherford** is the scientist associated with the discovery of the atomic nucleus.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dmitri Mendeleev**:

 
 
• A Russian chemist who formulated the **Periodic Law** and created the first widely recognized **Periodic Table** of elements in **1869**.
 
• He famously left gaps for yet-to-be-discovered elements and predicted their properties based on their positions in the table.
 
 
 
• **John Dalton**:
 
 
• He pioneered the modern **Atomic Theory** in **1808**, proposing that all matter is composed of tiny, indivisible particles called **atoms**.
 
• His work established the **Law of Multiple Proportions** and laid the foundation for modern chemical calculations.
 
 
 
• **Robert Boyle**:
 
 
• Regarded as the first modern chemist, he is most famous for **Boyle's Law**, which defines the inverse relationship between the **pressure** and **volume** of a gas at a constant temperature.
 
• He was a founding member of the **Royal Society** and was instrumental in separating **chemistry** from alchemy.

questions.question: The asthenosphere plays an important role in plate movements because:

options.text: It forms the Earth’s magnetic field
It is made of water bodies
It is partially molten and allows plates to move
It is perfectly solid and rigid

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It is partially molten and allows plates to move**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **asthenosphere** is a highly viscous, mechanically weak, and **ductile** region of the Earth's upper mantle, situated just below the **lithosphere**.
 
• It typically extends from a depth of about **80 km to 200 km** below the Earth's surface, though it can reach as deep as **700 km** in certain regions.
 
• This layer exists in a **plastic** or **semi-fluid** state because the temperatures are high enough to cause **partial melting** of the rock (approximately 1% to 5% melt), reducing its overall rigidity.
 
• The **lithosphere**, which is composed of the crust and the rigid uppermost mantle, is broken into **tectonic plates** that 'float' and glide over the yielding material of the asthenosphere.
 
• **Convection currents** occurring within the asthenosphere serve as the primary driving force for **plate movements**, facilitating processes such as seafloor spreading and subduction.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lithosphere**:

 
 
• Characterized by its **brittle** and **rigid** nature compared to the layers below.
 
• It includes both **continental crust** and **oceanic crust**.
 
 
 
• **Outer Core**:
 
 
• The layer responsible for generating the **Earth's magnetic field** through the **geodynamo** process.
 
• Unlike the asthenosphere, the outer core is entirely **liquid** and composed mainly of **iron and nickel**.
 
 
 
• **Mantle Composition**:
 
 
• The asthenosphere is primarily composed of **peridotite**, an ultramafic rock rich in **magnesium** and **iron**.
 
• Seismic waves slow down when they hit the asthenosphere, a region often called the **Low Velocity Zone (LVZ)**, confirming its less-than-solid state.

questions.question: The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) was established under which law?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)** was established under the **Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985**, which was enacted by the **Parliament** in exercise of the powers conferred by **Article 323A** of the **Constitution of India**.
 
• **Article 323A** was inserted into the Constitution via the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, specifically authorizing the Parliament to provide for the adjudication of disputes relating to the recruitment and conditions of service of public servants.
 
• The **Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985** facilitates the setting up of a **Central Administrative Tribunal** for the Union and **State Administrative Tribunals (SATs)** for individual states to ensure **speedy** and **inexpensive justice**.
 
• The **Central Administrative Tribunal** was formally established on **November 1, 1985**, during the tenure of the **Rajiv Gandhi government**, with its principal bench located in **New Delhi**.
 
• The tribunal is a **statutory body** that functions as a specialized court to adjudicate service-related matters, thereby reducing the heavy pendency of cases in the **High Courts** and the **Supreme Court**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Constitutional Framework and Jurisdiction**:

 
 
• While **Article 323A** is dedicated exclusively to administrative tribunals for public service matters, **Article 323B** provides for the establishment of tribunals for other matters like **taxation**, **labor**, and **land reforms**.
 
• The jurisdiction of **CAT** extends to the **All-India Services**, the **Central Civil Services**, civil posts under the Centre, and civilian employees of the **defense services**.
 
• Members of the **regular defense forces**, officers and servants of the **Supreme Court**, and the secretarial staff of the **Parliament** are specifically excluded from its jurisdiction.
 
 
 
• **Composition and Procedural Nature**:
 
 
• The tribunal is a **multi-member body** consisting of a **Chairman** and several **Members** drawn from both **Judicial** and **Administrative** backgrounds to provide balanced expertise.
 
• The tribunal is not bound by the rigid procedure prescribed in the **Code of Civil Procedure, 1908**; instead, it is guided by the **Principles of Natural Justice**.
 
• Following the landmark **L. Chandra Kumar Case (1997)**, the **Supreme Court** ruled that orders of the **CAT** are subject to the **judicial review** of the **High Courts** under **Article 226/227**.

questions.question: How many control characters are included in the original 7-bit ASCII standard?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**32**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **ASCII**, which stands for **American Standard Code for Information Interchange**, is a character encoding standard that uses **7 bits** to represent each character.
 
• A **7-bit** system allows for a total of **128 unique characters** (2⁷ = 128), ranging from decimal values **0 to 127**.
 
• Within this set, the **original standard** specifically designates a block of **32 control characters** located at the beginning of the character map.
 
• These **32 control characters** occupy decimal positions **0 through 31** (hexadecimal 00 to 1F) and are primarily **non-printable**.
 
• The purpose of these codes is to manage **hardware devices** and data streams; for instance, **CR (Carriage Return)** at 13 and **LF (Line Feed)** at 10 are used to control text formatting on printers and screens.
 
• Other notable control characters include **NUL (Null)** at 0, **TAB (Horizontal Tab)** at 9, and **ESC (Escape)** at 27, all of which provide functional instructions rather than visual symbols.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **ASCII Character Categories**:

 
 
• **Printable Characters**: There are **95 printable characters** in the 7-bit ASCII standard, ranging from decimal **32 to 126**. This group includes the **space character**, punctuation marks, digits **0-9**, and both **uppercase and lowercase** English alphabets.
 
• **The DEL Character**: Decimal **127** represents the **Delete (DEL)** character. While it is non-printable, it is often categorized separately from the primary **32-character control block** (0-31).
 
• **Extended ASCII**: To support more characters, an **8-bit version** was developed, doubling the capacity to **256 characters**. This allows for additional mathematical symbols, graphical elements, and foreign language characters.
 
• **Evolution to Unicode**: Modern computing has largely transitioned to **Unicode (UTF-8)**, which maintains the original **ASCII table** as its first 128 entries to ensure **backward compatibility** with older systems and files.

questions.question: In standard Windows Sleep mode on a laptop, where is the current session primarily stored while the machine is idle?

options.text: In RAM, which remains powered with a small amount of electricity

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**In RAM, which remains powered with a small amount of electricity**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Sleep Mode**, technically referred to as the **S3 sleep state** under the **ACPI (Advanced Configuration and Power Interface)** specification, is a low-power mode that allows a computer to quickly resume full operation.
 
• When a **Windows laptop** enters this mode, the **Operating System** saves the current working state, including all open **applications**, **files**, and **system metadata**, into the **RAM (Random Access Memory)**.
 
• Since **RAM** is **volatile memory**, it requires a constant flow of power to retain data; therefore, the system maintains a **trickle charge** or a small amount of electricity to the memory modules while cutting power to most other hardware components.
 
• The primary advantage of this mechanism is the **resume speed**, as the system does not need to reload data from the slower **storage drive** into the memory upon waking.
 
• If power is completely lost (e.g., battery dies) while in this mode, any unsaved data stored in the **RAM** is permanently lost because the **volatile storage** resets without power.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Comparison of Power States:
 
 
• **Hibernate Mode (S4 State)**: Saves the session to the **Hard Disk (HDD)** or **Solid State Drive (SSD)** in a file named **hiberfil.sys** and turns off the power entirely.
 
• **Hybrid Sleep**: A combination used mainly on desktops where the session is saved to both **RAM** and the **Hard Drive** to protect against power failure.
 
• **Modern Standby (S0 Low Power Idle)**: A newer state used in modern laptops that allows the system to stay connected to the internet and receive **notifications** even when the screen is off.
 
 
 
• Technical Limitations of Other Options:
 
 
• **System Drive**: Writing to the drive is a **non-volatile** process characteristic of **Hibernation**, not standard **Sleep**.
 
• **CPU Cache**: **L1**, **L2**, and **L3 caches** are extremely small (ranging from a few **kilobytes** to several **megabytes**) and cannot hold the **Gigabytes** of data required for a user session.
 
• **BIOS Chip**: The **ROM** or **Flash memory** on the **Motherboard** is reserved for **firmware** and **POST (Power-On Self-Test)** instructions and lacks the capacity or speed for session storage.

questions.question: The President of India’s “pocket veto” refers to:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**keeping a bill pending indefinitely**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Pocket Veto** is a constitutional power exercised by the **President of India** whereby they neither give assent to a bill nor return it for reconsideration to the **Parliament**.
 
• Under **Article 111** of the **Indian Constitution**, the President has three choices regarding a bill: grant assent, withhold assent, or return it (if it is not a **Money Bill**). However, the Constitution does not specify any **time limit** within which the President must take action.
 
• Because there is no prescribed duration for the President to act, they can simply keep the bill on their desk for an **indefinite period**, effectively preventing the bill from becoming an **Act**.
 
• This veto is called 'pocket' because the President metaphorically puts the bill in their pocket and forgets about it, as the **Constitution** is silent on the urgency of the decision.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Veto Powers of the Indian President**:

 
 
• **Absolute Veto**: The power of the President to say 'no' to a bill passed by **Parliament**. The bill then ends and does not become an act. This is usually used for **Private Members' Bills**.
 
• **Suspensive Veto**: The President exercises this by returning a bill for reconsideration. If **Parliament** passes the bill again with a **simple majority** (with or without amendments), the President is bound to give assent. This veto cannot be used for **Money Bills**.
 
• **Historical Instance**: In **1986**, President **Giani Zail Singh** exercised the pocket veto with respect to the **Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill**, which the government of **Rajiv Gandhi** had passed, as it was criticized for violating the privacy of correspondence.
 
• **Comparison**: In the **USA**, the President must return a bill within **10 days**; thus, the **Indian President** has a wider scope for the pocket veto because of the absence of a constitutional deadline.
